n: Jehoram (Joram), Ahab’s second son to reign, rules Israel for twelve years (about 852–841 BC). He will be the last king of Omri’s dynasty.
He was evil, though not as bad as his parents: he removed the sacred pillar of Baal Ahab had set up. Partial reform is better than none, but it is not repentance.

f.g: a standing stone or sacred pillar dedicated to Baal.

n: He held on to Jeroboam’s golden-calf worship, which every northern king kept as state policy.
Mesha of Moab was a breeder of sheep and paid Israel a huge annual tribute in lambs and wool. Mesha’s own inscription, the Moabite Stone (about 840 BC), names him and describes Israel’s domination.

f.g: known from the Moabite (Mesha) Stone, discovered in 1868.

n: When Ahab died, Mesha stopped paying and rebelled.
Jehoram musters Israel’s army to bring Moab back under control.
He asks Jehoshaphat of Judah to join him, and Jehoshaphat agrees with the same words he used with Ahab.
They choose to attack from the south, swinging around the Dead Sea through Edom, which was under Judah’s control.
The three kings—Israel, Judah, and Edom—march seven days by a roundabout route and run out of water for the army and animals.

f.g: made a circuit, took a roundabout route.

n: Jehoram despairs, blaming the Lord for bringing them out to die—oddly invoking the Lord he does not serve.
Jehoshaphat asks for a true prophet. An officer mentions Elisha, “who poured water on Elijah’s hands”—that is, Elijah’s personal servant.

f.w: poured water on the hands of Elijah

n: Jehoshaphat recognizes Elisha as a true prophet. Remarkably, the three kings go to the prophet rather than summoning him.
Elisha rebuffs Jehoram: “Why come to me? Go to your parents’ prophets!” Jehoram insists the Lord has brought them into danger.

f.w: What have I to do with thee?

n: Elisha says he helps only out of respect for faithful Jehoshaphat. A righteous person’s presence can bring blessings to others.
Elisha calls for a musician. As the music plays, the power of the Lord comes upon him. Music often prepares the heart to receive the Spirit.

f.w: the hand of the LORD came upon him

n: The command is strange: dig the dry valley full of trenches or pools. Faith often requires preparing for a blessing before it arrives.

f.g: pits or trenches to hold water.

n: There will be no wind or rain, yet the valley will fill with water for people and animals.
Water is easy for the Lord; He will also give them victory over Moab.

Elisha foretells a total campaign: they will destroy cities, cut trees, stop wells, and ruin fields with stones. (The law forbade cutting fruit trees during a siege; this was likely a special decree, or reflects the harshness of the war.)
At the time of the morning offering at the temple, water flows in from Edom—perhaps from a distant storm—and fills the land.

f.g: the grain offering made each morning.

n: Moab mobilizes every man old enough to bear arms and takes position on the border.
Early sunlight on the water, perhaps over red soil, makes the pools look like blood to the Moabites.
They assume the three allied kings have turned on each other and rush to loot the camp.
Instead, Israel’s army strikes and routs them, chasing them deep into Moab.
The allies devastate Moab as Elisha foretold. Only the capital, Kir-haraseth, holds out, though slingers bombard it.

f.g: Moab’s fortified capital, modern Kerak in Jordan.
soldiers who hurled stones with slings.

n: Desperate, Mesha tries to break out with seven hundred swordsmen toward the king of Edom’s position, but fails.

In a horrifying act, Mesha sacrifices his crown prince on the city wall to his god Chemosh. Something—a “great wrath”—then turns the campaign, and the allies withdraw. The text is brief and its meaning debated: perhaps the allies were horrified, or demoralized, or divine displeasure fell on Israel.

f.w: offered him for a burnt offering

f.g: great wrath; the Hebrew does not say whose.
